### Motivation

We are a group of passionate movie enthusiasts who are eager to dive into the Letterboxd dataset to uncover fascinating insights about films. In an era dominated by short-form content and claims of shorter attention spans, we are curious to see if shorter movies tend to receive higher ratings. We also want to explore the secret formulas behind top-rated films: Do certain directors excel when they stick to a specific genre or keep their films under 90 minutes? Beyond that, we are excited to analyze trends in genre preferences and discover what kind of film would captivate audiences.

### Additional Analysis: Linear Models 

Across several regression analyses, our primary objective was to assess how individual movie characteristics relate to a film’s average rating on Letterboxd. We first examined Runtime as a predictor and found that longer runtime was statistically associated with higher ratings. However when looked at visually looked at there was a suggested a weak linear trend. Even when applying a log-transformation or dichotomizing runtime into short (<90 minutes) and long (≥90 minutes) films, runtime remained a difficult variable to model on it's own.This suggests that runtime on its own provides limited insight into what drives audience reception.

Next, we explored alternative predictors that reflect audience engagement, appearances on user-curated lists, total watches, and number of fans. All three variables were highly statistically significant predictors of average rating, and were driven by the very large sample sizes. Effect sizes also were varied, with appearances in user-curated lists explaining the greatest proportion of variation in ratings (R² ≈ 0.15), followed by total watches (R² ≈ 0.083) and fans (R² ≈ 0.068). These findings indicate that movies that are more widely circulated and recommended within the platform tend to earn higher ratings which is possibly due to how many platforms make individual recommendations for its viewers. 

Finally, incorporating multiple predictors into an adjusted model resulted in improved model performance, with the adjusted runtime model explaining approximately 19% of the variance in average ratings, the strongest result among all models evaluated. Cross-validation further supported this conclusion, as the covariate-adjusted runtime model yielded the lowest RMSE, indicating the highest predictive accuracy. Altogether, while runtime alone is a weak predictor of perceived movie quality, audience engagement metrics, particularly curated list appearances, emerge as more powerful indicators of how viewers rate the movie. 

### Discussion

Overall, our findings suggest that while several movie characteristics are statistically associated with average ratings. Runtime alone showed a significant but very weak association with higher ratings and lacked a clearly linear visual pattern, which makes it not a great stand alone predictor. In contrast, appearances on user-curated lists, total watches, and fans all explained a much greater share of the variance, suggesting that movies with higher visibility and stronger community traction tend to receive higher ratings. The adjusted model that combined all the variables mentioned performed the best which supports our idea that the more popular a film is the better ratings it will have. 

However, our analysis has limitations which include effect sizes are on the smaller side even though there statistical significance driven by a large sample size. There is the possibility that these predictors may be a source of multicolinearity with underlying factors such as genre, marketing, or release year, and the dataset includes only English-language films. All these factors limit generalizability across global cinema and other genres of media. Future work could incorporate additional film attributes and nonlinear modeling techniques to better capture what contributes to audience reception and rating behavior.
